st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source establishes binding rules for legal paraprofessionals, alternative business structures and supervision of nonlawyers. Although its emphasis on professional oversight and internal controls is tangentially relevant, it does not address AI capability, task selection, verification, selective deployment or AI-driven work redesign, so its position on the cluster’s proposition cannot be determined.

[2] Paragraph (a) requires lawyers with managerial authority within a firm to make reasonable efforts to establish internal policies and procedures designed to provide reasonable assurance that all lawyers in the firm will conform to the Rules of Professional Conduct.

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: The Arizona framework accepts the cluster’s core distinction between continuing supervisory responsibility and automatic liability, while materially extending it to licensed ABSs, nonlawyer ownership and outsourced assistance. It requires lawyer-led, proportionate compliance systems and limits responsibility for another’s misconduct to ordering, knowing ratification or a knowing failure to take timely remedial action. It is regulatory guidance rather than AI-specific or empirical evidence.
qs: The degree of supervision required is that which is reasonable under the circumstances, taking into account factors such as the experience of the person who is being supervised and the amount of work supervised.

(1) the lawyer orders or, with the knowledge of the specific conduct, ratifies the conduct involved; or     (2) the lawyer is a partner or has comparable managerial authority in the firm in which the person is employed, or has direct supervisory authority over the person, and knows of the conduct at a time when its consequences can be avoided or mitigated but fails to take reasonable remedial action.

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s distinction between ABS ownership and permission to practise: Arizona permits ABS entities while requiring each legal-service provider to be licensed or otherwise authorized. It also specifies safeguards for lawyer independence, client interests and confidentiality, supporting the cluster’s account of entity-level oversight rather than deregulation without accountability. It does not provide evidence that ABS reform improves access to justice.
qs: No alternative business structure shall employ any person to provide legal services in the State of Arizona unless the person is licensed to practice law or otherwise authorized to provide legal services under Rule 31.1 or 31.3.

st.t: Legal payments: Convenience cannot weaken client safeguards
st.an: The Arizona source directly supports conditional modernization: it includes legal paraprofessionals and accommodates credit-card and mixed-ownership transactions while preserving trust-account segregation, nonclient allocation of chargeback risk, internal controls, reconciliation and practitioner accountability. It provides regulatory requirements, not evidence that the framework is effective in practice.
qs: Funds belonging in whole or in part to a client or third person in connection with a representation shall be kept separate and apart from the lawyer’s or legal paraprofessional’s personal and business accounts.

st.t: Licensed alternatives: Expanded practice retains accountability
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that expanded legal-service models can retain licensing and accountability. Arizona assigns formal licensing responsibility for alternative business structures and legal paraprofessionals and subjects both categories to Supreme Court disciplinary oversight. It provides operative regulatory design, not evidence that the framework improves access, cost or quality.

Any person licensed as a legal paraprofessional is subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Arizona Supreme Court and the authority delegated in these rules to the board of governors of the state bar.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s regulatory-accountability component by showing that Arizona extends distinct disciplinary and sanction mechanisms to alternative business structures and legal paraprofessionals. It supplies concrete evidence of safeguards, but no empirical evidence that these reforms improve access, service quality or legal outcomes.

kp.k: Court adopts legal-services reforms effective January 2021
kp.d: The Arizona Supreme Court's August 27, 2020 order adopts new practice-authorization and entity-regulation rules, changes professional-conduct and disciplinary rules, and establishes a legal-paraprofessional evidentiary privilege, effective January 1, 2021. This is primary regulatory material, not an AI study: it contains no findings or predictions about AI adoption, productivity or employment.
qs: ORDER AMENDING                   THE ARIZONA RULES OF THE SUPREME COURT                      AND THE ARIZONA RULES OF EVIDENCE
effective January 1, 2021

kp.k: Licensed entities may include nonlawyer ownership and management
kp.d: Rule 31.1(c) authorizes an alternative business structure with nonlawyer economic interests or decision-making authority to engage lawyers to serve third parties, conditional on ACJA § 7-209 licensing, employment of at least one active Arizona lawyer in good standing supervising practice under ER 5.3, and provision of services only by authorized persons. Entity ownership and authorization to perform legal work remain distinct.
qs: An entity that includes nonlawyers who have an economic interest or decision-making authority as defined in ACJA 7-209 may employ, associate with, or engage a lawyer or lawyers to provide legal services to third parties only if:
it employs at least one person who is an active member in good standing of the State Bar of Arizona under Rule 32 who supervises the practice of law under ER 5.3;
legal services are only provided by persons authorized to do so and in compliance with the Rules of Supreme Court.

kp.k: Licensing balances access with independence and client protection
kp.d: Rule 33.1 establishes an eleven-member Committee on Alternative Business Structures to examine applications and recommend licensing decisions to the Court. Regulatory objectives include public protection, access to legal services, the rule of law and a strong, diverse profession. Applicants' governance must safeguard independent legal judgment, standards of work, clients' interests and confidentiality. These are licensing objectives and requirements, not demonstrated access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: The Committee on Alternative Business Structures shall consist of eleven members.
promoting access to legal services;
encouraging an independent, strong, diverse, and effective legal profession;
lawyers providing legal services to consumers act with independence consistent with the lawyers’ professional responsibilities;
the lawyer makes decisions in the best interest of clients;

kp.k: Practice authorization remains bounded despite structural liberalization
kp.d: Rules 31–31.3 retain the Court's jurisdiction over authorized and unauthorized practice. Practice includes legal opinions, representation, filing documents for specific persons, negotiation of legal rights and preparation of rights-affecting documents. Limited exceptions cover specified governmental, business, tax and other activities; nonlawyer participation is not a general permission to supply legal services.
qs: The Arizona Supreme Court has jurisdiction over any person or entity engaged in the authorized or unauthorized “practice of law” in Arizona, as that phrase is defined in (b).
negotiating legal rights or responsibilities on behalf of a specific person or entity;
preparing a document, in any medium, intended to affect or secure a specific person’s or entity’s legal rights.
a person or entity may engage in the practice of law in a limited manner as authorized in Rule 31.3(b) through (e)

kp.k: Legal paraprofessionals receive a regulated service-provider role
kp.d: Rule 31.3(e)(4) permits certified legal document preparers and legal paraprofessionals to perform services in compliance with the Arizona Code of Judicial Administration. Rule 32 makes legal paraprofessionals affiliate State Bar members for regulation and discipline, with examination and licensing administered by the Administrative Office of Courts under ACJA § 7-210. The order does not itself reproduce that code's detailed practice scope or qualifications.
qs: Certified legal document preparers and legal paraprofessionals may perform services in compliance with the Arizona Code of Judicial Administration.
Legal paraprofessionals are affiliate members for purposes of regulation and discipline under these rules.
Examination and licensure of legal paraprofessionals shall be administered by the Administrative Office of Courts as provided in ACJA § 7-210.

kp.k: Professional safeguards extend across multidisciplinary firms
kp.d: The amended ER 1.0 commentary treats an organization providing legal, accounting and financial-planning services as a firm for professional-conduct purposes. Lawyers must assure reasonable safeguards for confidences and conflicts across employees, officers, directors and owners, including nonlawyers who do not provide legal services. ER 1.10 extends conflict imputation to lawyers and nonlawyers and to legal and nonlegal matters, subject to its personal-interest exception.
qs: an organization that provides legal, accounting, and financial planning services to clients is a “firm” for purposes of these Rules
regardless of whether or not the nonlawyers participate in providing legal services.

While lawyers and nonlawyers are associated in a firm, none of them shall knowingly represent a client on legal or nonlegal matters when any one of them practicing alone would be prohibited from doing so by ERs 1.7 or 1.9

kp.k: Common ownership restricts adverse representations across firms
kp.d: ER 1.7(c) prohibits asserting a claim against a party represented by another firm when the same person or entity has a direct or indirect ownership interest of 10 percent or more in both firms, or comparable managerial authority in both. The commentary states that this bar applies irrespective of consent; lesser overlaps are assessed under the ordinary concurrent-conflict rules.
qs: A lawyer may not represent a party in asserting a claim against another party represented by a firm if the same person or entity holds an ownership interest, directly or indirectly, of 10 percent or more, or has managerial authority comparable to that of a partner, in the lawyer’s firm and the other firm.
ER 1.7(c) parallels ER 1.7(b)(3) in barring certain concurrent representations of adverse parties, irrespective of consent.

kp.k: Screening exceptions exclude nonlawyer owners and senior leadership
kp.d: ER 1.10(f) allows screening of a personally disqualified nonlawyer without imputing the disqualification to the firm, except where the nonlawyer is an owner, shareholder, partner, officer or director. A parallel rule applies to lawyers disqualified by pre-licensure conduct. Screening requires timely measures, including restricted information access, notices and reminders.
qs: If a nonlawyer is personally disqualified pursuant to paragraph (a), the nonlawyer may be screened and the nonlawyer’s personal disqualification is not imputed to the rest of the firm unless the nonlawyer is an owner, shareholder, partner, officer, or director of the firm.
Screening measures must be implemented as soon as practical after a lawyer, nonlawyer, or firm knows or reasonably should know that there is a need for screening.

kp.k: Lawyers must prevent nonlawyer interference with professional judgment
kp.d: ER 5.3 requires policies preventing nonlawyers from directing, controlling or materially limiting independent judgment or materially influencing client selection. Firms with nonlawyer economic interests or managerial authority must identify a lawyer responsible for compliance policies. The commentary expressly treats legal services provided by a lawyer through an unlicensed ABS as unauthorized practice.
qs: to prevent nonlawyers in a firm from directing, controlling, or materially limiting the lawyer’s independent professional judgment on behalf of clients or materially influencing which clients a lawyer does or does not represent;

When a firm includes nonlawyers who have an economic interest or managerial authority in the firm, any lawyer practicing therein shall ensure that a lawyer has been identified as responsible for establishing policies and procedures within the firm to assure nonlawyer compliance with these rules.
Any lawyer who provides legal services through an unlicensed ABS is engaged in the unauthorized practice of law.

kp.k: Supervision duties encompass external nonlawyer service providers
kp.d: ER 5.3 requires reasonable supervision of nonlawyers assisting legal work inside or outside the firm, including ethical instruction and confidentiality protections. Directions to external providers must fit the circumstances. Where clients select providers, lawyers ordinarily should agree with clients how monitoring responsibility is allocated. These are human service-provider supervision rules, not express AI-verification requirements.
qs: A lawyer having supervisory authority over a nonlawyer within or outside a firm shall make reasonable efforts to ensure that the nonlawyer’s conduct when engaged in activities assisting lawyers in providing legal services is compatible with the professional obligations of the lawyer.

Where the client directs the selection of a particular nonlawyer service provider outside the firm, the lawyer ordinarily should agree with the client concerning the allocation of responsibility for monitoring as between the client and the lawyer.

kp.k: Joint firm fees require disclosure and reasonable responsibility
kp.d: The revised ER 1.5(e) permits firms jointly working on a matter to divide client fees with written disclosure of fee and responsibility allocations, signed client consent, a reasonable total fee and a reasonable division of responsibility supporting complete and diligent representation. This regulates collaborative billing arrangements rather than prescribing hourly, fixed-fee or value-based pricing.
qs: Two or more firms jointly working on a matter may divide a fee paid by a client if:
the firms disclose to the client in writing how the fee will be divided and how the firms will divide responsibility for the matter among themselves;
the division of responsibility among firms is reasonable in light of the client’s need that the entire representation be completely and diligently completed.

kp.d: ER 1.0's business-transaction definition includes related goods or services sold to existing legal clients, referrals to nonlegal services within a firm or financially connected entity, and acceptance of nonmonetary property or client-business interests as fees. ER 1.8(m) requires compliance with both ER 1.7 and ER 1.8(a) when clients expect representation in the transaction or the lawyer's financial interest materially risks limiting representation.
qs: the sale of goods or services related to the practice of law to existing clients of a firm’s legal practice;
transactions between a lawyer or a firm and a client in which a lawyer or firm accepts nonmonetary property or an interest in the client's business as payment of all or part of a fee.
A lawyer wishing to engage in a business transaction with a client must comply with both ER 1.7 and 1.8(a)

kp.k: Practice sales preserve client choice and existing fee arrangements
kp.d: ER 1.17 requires notice identifying the purchaser, the client's right to other counsel or possession of the file, and presumed consent to file transfer after ninety days without action or objection. It prohibits financing a sale through increased client fees, requires honoring existing fee and scope arrangements, and imposes competence, confidentiality and conflict safeguards on participating lawyers.
qs: the client's right to retain other counsel or to take possession of the file;
the client's consent to the transfer of the client's files will be presumed if the client does not take any action or does not otherwise object within ninety (90) days of receipt of the notice.
A sale may not be financed by increases in fees charged to the clients of the practice.
Existing arrangements between the seller and the client as to fees and the scope of the work must be honored by the purchaser.

kp.k: Disciplinary accountability includes entities and legal paraprofessionals
kp.d: The order extends disciplinary jurisdiction to ABSs and their members and to licensed legal paraprofessionals. ER 8.3 adds reporting obligations for known misconduct raising substantial compliance questions, subject to confidentiality protections. Its commentary distinguishes lawyers retained to represent an ABS from lawyers working in or owning it: the latter remain subject to the reporting duty. Unauthorized-practice sanctions include a civil penalty up to $25,000 when another sanction is imposed.
qs: Any alternative business structure and its members are subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Arizona Supreme Court.
Any person licensed as a legal paraprofessional is subject to the disciplinary jurisdiction of the Arizona Supreme Court
does not apply to a lawyer retained to represent the ABS but does apply to lawyers who work in or have ownership interests in an ABS.
The superior court may order a civil penalty up to $25,000 against every respondent upon whom another sanction is imposed.

kp.k: Paraprofessional clients receive privilege and financial safeguards
kp.d: New Evidence Rule 513 grants confidential legal-advice communications with legal paraprofessionals protection co-extensive with attorney-client privilege. Amended Rule 43 extends client-fund separation, recordkeeping and reconciliation requirements to legal paraprofessionals. Rule 32 also requires affiliate members to disclose private-practice and professional-liability-insurance status, with information made publicly available; this is disclosure, not a universal insurance mandate.
qs: A communication between a legal paraprofessional and a client is privileged if it is made for the purpose of securing or giving legal advice, is made in confidence, and is treated confidentially.
This privilege is co-extensive with, and affords the same protection as, the attorney-client privilege.

Funds belonging in whole or in part to a client or third person in connection with a representation shall be kept separate and apart from the lawyer’s or legal paraprofessional’s personal and business accounts.

A lawyer or legal paraprofessional shall make or cause to be made a monthly three-way reconciliation of the client ledgers, trust account general ledger or register, and the trust account bank statement.
